accuracy.evidence: Uses the Year 1 measurement statements in the English national curriculum: compare, describe and solve practical problems for time (quicker, slower, earlier, later) and measure and begin to record time. All the clap counts were checked: brushing teeth 8 against a candle 1, the song and tidy up both 6, the snack starts at 5 and lasts 3 so it ends at 8 while the bath lasts 6, Mia 4 is quicker than Sam 7, and sneeze 1, shoes 3 and lunch 9 are in order.

misconceptions.evidence: Takes on the belief that whatever ends last took longest (the snack starts late at clap 5 and must be slid back to the start line before comparing with the bath), confusing quicker with more (Mia's 4 claps against Sam's 7), and thinking two jobs cannot take the same time (dragging tidy up to exactly 6 claps). The adult notes name all three slips as common mistakes.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagdur is a clap timeline: horizontal job bars grow from one start line while a play head ticks 0 to 10 claps, one bar end can be dragged to change a duration, and one bar can be slid to line up a late start. It passes the 30% shingle gate and differs from the clock-face labs (hour and half hour hands) and the ordering-events lab (cards in a sequence).

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step changes one idea on the same timeline: two jobs start together and the one still going takes longer, two bars matched to the same count take the same time, a late start is lined up before comparing, fewer claps means quicker in a race, and then three jobs go shortest to longest. The Challenge asks the same ideas with new everyday jobs.

predictions.evidence: Five of the six steps ask for a prediction before the child acts (which takes longer, which takes longer when the snack ends last, who is quicker, and so on). The pick is locked in, and the feedback quotes it back, for example 'You predicted The bath: spot on!' or explains why the guess missed.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six Challenge questions each have their own reason in the why() replies, for example 'A sneeze is over in a moment, a night of sleep goes on for hours' and 'Fewer claps means quicker'. A wrong answer explains the slip instead of just saying 'try again'. A short rule card (line up the starts, the one still going takes longer, fewer claps is quicker) stays above the questions.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs come out at about Flesch-Kincaid grade 0 with short sentences and words like longer, shorter, quicker and slower. The adult notes are at grade 6.8 and quote the curriculum wording. Lab step text is two or three short sentences, and the tasks start with a pointing hand and a verb (Press Play, Slide the snack).

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph does a job. The kid text gives the start-together rule, counting claps, quicker and slower, and late starts. The adult text covers the curriculum link, the three named mistakes, what each lab step does and a practical family timer game. There is no generic praise or padding, and the content gate's similarity is under 12%.

mobile.evidence: Checked at 390 px on iPhone and Android in light and dark. Bars are full width with labels above, and the clap count goes inside the bar when the bar reaches the right edge. The job buttons are big pill buttons at least 44 px tall in a wrap row, and drag handles have a large hit area. Nothing scrolls sideways, and the clap ruler fits on screen.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas has an aria-label, and every drag has a button version (Slide snack and plus or minus 1 clap). The live caption describes each state in words ('Tidy up takes 6 claps, the same as the song'). Colour is never the only cue because each bar is named and labelled with its claps. Contrast passes in both themes, and the sound is off by default with a toggle.

sources: Department for Education (2013) National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study, Key Stage 1, Year 1 Measurement (time statements)
NCETM Mastery professional development materials, Measurement: comparing and ordering durations (Year 1)
Piaget (1946, English translation 1969) The Child's Conception of Time: young children judge which lasted longer by where things stopped rather than by start and end together
